w: What's tested How PTH controls calcium and phosphate, and which PTH fragments are active The normal parathyroid: chief and oxyphil cells, and the fat-to-cell ratio by age Primary hyperparathyroidism: adenoma versus hyperplasia versus carcinoma, the classic symptoms, surgery, the sestamibi scan and intraoperative PTH Secondary hyperparathyroidism and its causes Hypoparathyroidism (causes, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, dental root hypoplasia) and pseudohypoparathyroidism The three zones of the adrenal cortex: salt, sugar, sex Cushing syndrome and its lab logic: cortisol read with ACTH Hyperaldosteronism: Conn syndrome (renin low) versus secondary (renin high) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: 21-hydroxylase and 17-hydroxylase deficiency Addison disease, and adrenal cortical adenoma and carcinoma The adrenal medulla: pheochromocytoma (the rule of 10s, Zellballen) and neuroblastoma Dr. Melad Dababneh, a head and neck pathologist, gave this second endocrine pathology lecture on November 4 (his deck is based on Dr. Bell's lecture): the parathyroid first, then the adrenal cortex and medulla. His thread through the lecture is that every gland runs on negative feedback, so for each disease ask whether the problem is primary, in the gland itself, or secondary, something else driving it, and read the hormone together with its driver. Parathyroid function: PTH, calcium and phosphate The four small parathyroid glands sit behind the thyroid and control calcium and phosphate. The loop is ordinary negative feedback. When serum calcium falls, the glands release parathyroid hormone, PTH. PTH raises calcium in two places. In the bone, it increases bone turnover, so calcium is released into the blood. In the kidney, it increases calcium reabsorption, decreases phosphate reabsorption, so more phosphate is dumped in the urine, and increases production of active vitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D. As serum calcium rises, it switches the glands off. Dr. Dababneh's shorthand: PTH takes back calcium and dumps phosphate. Keep that pair in mind, because every parathyroid disease in this lecture is read through it. Like any hormone, PTH is eventually metabolized by the liver and kidney. It circulates as pieces of its amino acid chain, and the two ends behave differently: Intact PTH and N-terminal fragments are biologically active, have a short half-life of minutes, and are metabolized by the liver and kidney. C-terminal fragments are biologically inactive, have a long half-life of several hours, and are cleared by glomerular filtration. The short half-life of active PTH is what lets surgeons measure PTH during an operation and know within minutes whether the overactive gland is out. The normal parathyroid under the microscope The parathyroid is a neuroendocrine organ, so it looks like other neuroendocrine tissue, such as the C cells of the thyroid or the cells of the pituitary: the cells grow in nests, and their nuclei have speckled salt and pepper chromatin. There are two cell types. Chief cells look clear to bluish, and can be completely clear. Oxyphil cells look pink. Between the nests is a lot of fat, the white spaces on the slide. The amount of fat changes with age, and Dr. Dababneh gave a rule of thumb: subtract the person's age from 100 to get the expected percent of cells. Someone in their twenties has a gland that is mostly cells with a little fat. In a 70-year-old, about 70 percent of the gland should be fat and about 30 percent cells. So if a gland from someone in their fifties or sixties is about 80 percent cells, it is hypercellular, and a hypercellular gland may be hyperfunctioning. He gave a second example: a middle-aged man whose gland is about 70 percent cells has hypercellular parathyroid tissue. In class it came out as "subtract 100 from your age"; the rule is 100 minus the age. He also said "thyroid" a couple of times in this part where he meant parathyroid. Primary hyperparathyroidism Primary hyperparathyroidism is PTH secretion that is inappropriately high for the serum calcium, without a known stimulus driving it: the gland itself is the problem. Excess PTH pulls calcium out of the bones and holds it in at the kidney, so the patient has high calcium. It is common: about 1 in 1,000 people, and 1 in 500 women over 45, with a mean age of 58. There are three causes: parathyroid adenoma, parathyroid hyperplasia and parathyroid carcinoma. The symptoms come from the high calcium. The classic picture has three parts: renal calculi, kidney stones, since most stones are calcium-heavy; bone disorders such as osteitis fibrosa cystica, because bone is broken down for its calcium and weakens; and neuromuscular abnormalities, because calcium disturbs muscle contraction and the muscles feel tired. Dr. Dababneh's memory aid was "stones, bones and groans" (he stumbled over it in class). Today, though, most patients have no symptoms: the high calcium is found on a routine blood chemistry panel. Parathyroid adenoma An adenoma means one of the four glands undergoes neoplastic proliferation, forms a mass and overproduces PTH. It is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism, 80 to 90 percent of cases. It is a benign neoplasm of chief cells or oxyphil cells, three times more common in women, usually in the fourth to fifth decade. It is a solitary lesion, the lower glands are involved more often, and it weighs about 0.3 to 1.0 grams. Under the microscope, a rim of normal background parathyroid with its fat sits beside a chunk of cellular tissue with no fat. That chunk is the adenoma, an overgrowth of a single cell type, which may be pink oxyphil cells or clear chief cells. Primary chief cell hyperplasia Hyperplasia causes 10 to 15 percent of primary hyperparathyroidism. Here all four glands are enlarged. The slide says the enlargement may be asymmetric, and Dr. Dababneh added that it is usually symmetric. The combined weight is usually 1 to 3 grams. The glands have increased parenchymal cell mass with decreased stromal fat: sheets or nodules of chief cells, oncocytic cells or both, with little fat between them. Unlike an adenoma, the increase in cells is not necessarily neoplastic or clonal. Telling adenoma from hyperplasia This is a point he made carefully: adenoma and hyperplasia cannot be told apart by laboratory testing. Both are hyperfunctioning, both raise PTH and both cause hypercalcemia. The diagnosis needs anatomic evaluation: is it a single enlarged gland or several? Adenomas in all four glands are very rare, so four enlarged glands is most likely hyperplasia, while an adenoma is usually solitary. Dr. Dababneh: "Adenomas and hyperplasias cannot be distinguished only on lab testing. Both of them will be hyperfunctioning, both of them will have increased parathyroid hormone levels." Parathyroid carcinoma Parathyroid carcinoma is the malignant counterpart of the adenoma: it invades the surrounding structures and vessels. It is very rare (he said he has probably seen one), and most common in the fifth and sixth decades. Its clue is the size of the metabolic problem: very high, symptomatic hypercalcemia, with calcium tending to run over 13. Grossly it is an ill-defined mass adherent to the adjacent soft tissues, the thyroid or the tissue around the esophagus, with a mean size of 3 centimeters and a mean weight of 6.7 grams. Under the microscope the nuclei are larger and more atypical, and pleomorphic, meaning they vary in size and shape. There is tumor necrosis, dusky pink areas where the cells are dying, and the tumor infiltrates neighboring structures. When cells die out inside a neoplasm, he said, it is usually a malignant process. If a single gland is enlarged, it is presumed to be an adenoma: the enlarged gland is removed and sent to pathology, and a grossly normal gland is biopsied. If several glands are enlarged, it is presumed to be hyperplasia, and three and a half glands are removed, leaving half a gland in the body to keep calcium in balance. Removed tissue can even be saved pending pathology and re-implanted elsewhere in the body, where it still functions. Because a parathyroid is so small it can look like a blob of fat, surgeons used to send the tissue for a frozen section, an intraoperative consultation: the pathologist freezes the tissue, cuts and stains it, and answers within about 20 minutes whether it is parathyroid. Now PTH can be measured during the operation instead. Preoperative localization uses a sestamibi scan, a radioactive tracer taken up by parathyroid tissue. At 15 minutes everything lights up; at 2 hours only the hyperfunctioning gland is still lit. That finds the adenoma before surgery, so the surgeon knows where to look. Intraoperative PTH testing uses a rapid intact PTH test with results in 15 to 20 minutes. If the surgery worked, PTH drops by more than 50 percent after the enlarged gland is removed. If nothing drops, the surgeon probably took the fat around the gland, or not all of the abnormal tissue. Together these make minimally invasive parathyroid surgery possible: localize the abnormal gland before surgery, measure a preoperative PTH, remove the gland through a small localized incision, then confirm with an intraoperative PTH. It works because most primary hyperparathyroidism is a single adenoma, and because the half-life of PTH is short. Secondary hyperparathyroidism Secondary hyperparathyroidism is overactivity of the parathyroids induced by conditions that cause chronic hypocalcemia. The glands respond to low calcium as they should, but the low calcium comes from disease. The most common cause is renal failure, because the failing kidney can no longer keep calcium in balance. Calcium and vitamin D deficiencies are the other causes. The glands become hyperplastic, usually all of them. The clinical features are similar to those of primary hyperparathyroidism, but less severe. When it is treated surgically, the operation is a three-and-a-half gland parathyroidectomy. But he stressed that the most important step is solving the primary issue: fix the vitamin D deficiency, and calcium and the parathyroids go back to normal. Hypoparathyroidism Hypoparathyroidism is low serum calcium due to underproduction of PTH. There are three groups of causes. Surgical: during a thyroidectomy the parathyroids can be removed with the thyroid, on purpose when a thyroid cancer invades one, or incidentally. Congenital absence: thymic aplasia, DiGeorge syndrome, in which patients lack both the thymus and the parathyroids. Autoimmune: hereditary polyglandular deficiency syndrome, which attacks the parathyroids much as Hashimoto disease attacks the thyroid. Because the thymus and parathyroids develop together, a parathyroid sometimes sits inside thymic tissue rather than in its usual place, and surgeons may send thymus to pathology to look for it. Without PTH, the kidney does the reverse of what PTH asks: it dumps calcium and keeps phosphate. So the labs show low calcium and high phosphate. Low calcium makes nerves and muscles irritable: tetany, convulsions, laryngospasm and paresthesias. Two classic exam signs come from the same irritability. Chvostek sign is a twitch of the facial muscles when the cheek is tapped. Trousseau sign is a spasm of the hand when the arm is compressed, as with a tourniquet or blood pressure cuff. Other findings are cataracts, dental root hypoplasia, spotty alopecia, nail fragility and basal ganglia calcification. On dental root hypoplasia, Dr. Dababneh: "important, no calcium." Pseudohypoparathyroidism Pseudo means false. The patient looks as if they have hypoparathyroidism, with low calcium and high phosphate, but the glands are fine: PTH is high. The problem is end-organ resistance to PTH: the target organs, such as the kidney, don't respond to the signal, so the glands keep pushing. Patients also have developmental anomalies, short stature, short metacarpals and metatarsals, and intellectual disability (the slide uses an older term). Before making the diagnosis, rule out renal failure, malabsorption and vitamin D deficiency, since those can also give low calcium with a high PTH. In class he described the kidney in this disease as having "kidney failure". He meant that the kidney fails to respond to PTH; true renal failure is one of the look-alikes the slide says to rule out. Primary hyperparathyroidism High High Low The gland overproduces with no stimulus Secondary hyperparathyroidism High Low or low-normal Not taught Renal failure, low calcium or vitamin D drive the glands Hypoparathyroidism Low Low High Too little PTH: surgery, DiGeorge, autoimmune Pseudohypoparathyroidism High Low High Target organs resist PTH The adrenal gland and the three zones of the cortex The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys, and each is shaped like a triangle. The outer, lighter, golden-yellow part is the cortex; the inner, pinker part is the medulla. The medulla is another neuroendocrine organ and makes catecholamines. The cortex makes three kinds of steroid hormone, and each kind has its own syndrome: too much cortisol is Cushing syndrome, too much aldosterone is hyperaldosteronism, androgen problems come with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and too little of everything is hypoadrenalism, Addison disease. The cortex has three layers. From the outside in: Zona glomerulosa: mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone, which controls salt. Zona fasciculata: glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol, sugar. Zona reticularis: mainly androgens, the sex steroids. The slide lists glucocorticoids and androgens for both inner zones; the fasciculata is mainly glucocorticoids and the reticularis mainly androgens. The memory aid from the book: it gets sweeter as you go from outside to inside, salt, sugar, sex. Dr. Dababneh often said "cortisone" in this part of the lecture. The hormone of the zona fasciculata, and the one measured in Cushing syndrome, is cortisol. Zona glomerulosa Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) Salt Hyperaldosteronism, Conn syndrome Zona fasciculata Cortisol (glucocorticoid) Sugar Cushing syndrome Zona reticularis Androgens (sex steroids) Sex Virilization, as in 21-hydroxylase deficiency Medulla Catecholamines Not part of the cortex Pheochromocytoma Cortisol and Cushing syndrome Cortisol secretion is stimulated by ACTH, adrenocorticotropic hormone from the pituitary, which travels to the adrenal cortex and asks it to release cortisol. Cortisol inhibits glucose uptake by cells, promotes fat deposition and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis. Each of those actions shows up in its excess. Excess cortisol is Cushing syndrome, and it has several sources. A pituitary tumor can overproduce ACTH, which drives the adrenal cortex into hyperplasia. A tumor of the adrenal cortex can make cortisol itself. An ectopic tumor, such as a lung cancer, can make ACTH as a paraneoplastic effect, just as some lung cancers make ADH. And many patients take oral steroid pills for many conditions, which can also produce the syndrome. The manifestations are central obesity, a buffalo hump, a round moon face, hyperglycemia, hirsutism and excess androgens, osteoporosis, psychiatric changes, hypertension and acne. To find the source, read cortisol together with ACTH, exactly as with the thyroid. If cortisol and ACTH are both high, ACTH is the driver: a pituitary tumor or an ectopic tumor such as a lung cancer. If the problem is primary in the adrenal cortex, the extra cortisol sends negative feedback to the pituitary and tells it to stop making ACTH, so cortisol is high but ACTH is low. On these two tests alone, the pituitary and ectopic sources look the same; the rest of the story, such as a lung mass, tells them apart. Dr. Dababneh: "Very similar to thyroid. Primary hyperthyroidism: T3, T4 high, TSH low. Primary Cushing: cortisol high, and the ACTH low. Secondary: both will be high." Pituitary tumor making ACTH High High ACTH drives both adrenals to make cortisol Ectopic tumor making ACTH (for example, lung cancer) High High Paraneoplastic ACTH drives the adrenals Adrenal tumor making cortisol High Low Cortisol feeds back and shuts off pituitary ACTH Aldosterone and the renin-angiotensin system Besides the adrenal cortex itself, aldosterone production is governed from the kidney through the renin-angiotensin system. Renin acts on angiotensinogen in the plasma to form angiotensin I; angiotensin converting enzyme, ACE, turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II; and angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone makes the kidney retain sodium and excrete potassium, which makes it the major regulator of fluid volume. Dr. Dababneh drew the parallel: just as PTH takes back calcium and dumps phosphate, aldosterone takes back sodium and dumps potassium. Too much aldosterone means too much salt, and too much salt means high blood pressure. Hyperaldosteronism: Conn syndrome versus secondary The clinical features of hyperaldosteronism are hypertension, fatigue, high sodium and low potassium. The question is where it starts. Primary hyperaldosteronism starts in the adrenal: an adrenal adenoma, which is Conn syndrome, or adrenocortical hyperplasia. Because the aldosterone comes from the cortex and not from the renin-angiotensin system, negative feedback on the kidney shuts renin down: aldosterone high, renin low. Secondary hyperaldosteronism starts at the kidney: congestive heart failure with diminished renal perfusion, or renal artery stenosis. The kidney isn't getting the blood it needs, so it overproduces renin, and renin drives aldosterone: aldosterone high, renin high. He added a renin-secreting tumor as another way to get the secondary pattern. "The same concept repeats itself, primary versus secondary." Where it starts The adrenal cortex The kidney, poorly perfused Causes Adrenal adenoma (Conn syndrome), adrenocortical hyperplasia Congestive heart failure, renal artery stenosis, a renin-secreting tumor Aldosterone High High Renin Low, shut off by feedback High, it is the driver Shared features Hypertension, fatigue, high sodium, low potassium Hypertension, fatigue, high sodium, low potassium Adrenal androgens and congenital adrenal hyperplasia Adrenal androgens are steroid hormones that are converted to testosterone in peripheral tissues, and they accentuate male characteristics. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a group of autosomal recessive disorders, each a defect in an enzyme involved in cortisol biosynthesis. Congenital means you are born with it; recessive means a defective copy has come from each parent. In the cortex, cholesterol is converted step by step into aldosterone, cortisol or androgens, with a different enzyme at each step. When one enzyme is missing, the steps before it pile up and the pathway shifts toward whatever can still be made. The clinical picture can include androgen excess or deficiency, defects in sodium metabolism and glucocorticoid deficiency. The most common form is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which has several variants. Losing 21-hydroxylase shuts down the path to the mineralocorticoids and the path to the glucocorticoids, so the whole pathway shifts into overproducing androgens. The result is androgen excess: clitoral hypertrophy, pseudohermaphroditism, oligomenorrhea, acne, hirsutism and precocious puberty. About one third of cases also have sodium wasting from aldosterone deficiency. A less common form is 17-hydroxylase deficiency. It causes androgen deficiency: no secondary sex characteristics in females and pseudohermaphroditism in males. Precursors with mineralocorticoid activity accumulate, so the patient has sodium retention and hypertension. The treatment for all forms is glucocorticoids, and it uses negative feedback. These patients are short of cortisol. Giving glucocorticoid tells the pituitary to cut ACTH, the hormone that drives the whole adrenal cortical pathway, so the pathway quiets down and the symptoms of androgen excess ease. Two slips from class: he said "both of the parents has to have it" (in an autosomal recessive disease each parent carries and passes on one defective copy), and he said the acne and hirsutism come from "overproduction of cortisone" (they come from excess androgens). He showed the full steroid pathway and said he had to memorize it for his own exams; what this lecture teaches from it is the effect of the 21- and 17-hydroxylase blocks. How common The most common form, several variants Less common Androgens Excess: clitoral hypertrophy, pseudohermaphroditism, oligomenorrhea, acne, hirsutism, precocious puberty Deficiency: no secondary sex characteristics in females, pseudohermaphroditism in males Sodium About a third waste sodium (aldosterone deficiency) Retained, from precursors with mineralocorticoid activity Blood pressure Low in salt wasters High Treatment Glucocorticoids Glucocorticoids Addison disease On the opposite side is hypoadrenalism. Chronic primary hypoadrenalism is Addison disease: the whole cortex shuts down, so the patient makes no glucocorticoids, no aldosterone and no androgens, and has a mix of all the deficiency symptoms. Without aldosterone, sodium is low, potassium is high and blood pressure is low. Without cortisol, glucose is low and there is fatigue and weakness. The full list on the slide: weakness, fatigue, low glucose, nausea and vomiting, weight loss, psychosis, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, low sodium, high potassium, high ACTH and an inability to withstand stress. ACTH is high because the problem is primary: with the cortex failing, feedback is lost and the pituitary keeps pushing. If the failure is secondary, at the pituitary, ACTH and the adrenal cortical hormones are both low. Causes: autoimmune destruction, 60 to 70 percent, the most common; viral infection, such as herpes, CMV and AIDS; chronic infection, fungal or tuberculosis; metastatic cancer, from the lung, breast or melanoma; and systemic disease, such as amyloidosis, sarcoidosis and hemochromatosis, in which iron or amyloid deposits in the cortex and shuts it down. Tumors of the adrenal cortex As anywhere else, a benign tumor of the cortex is an adenoma and a malignant one a carcinoma. Most adrenal cortical adenomas are nonsecreting, and the most common functional adenomas secrete aldosterone, giving high sodium, low potassium and hypertension. Adrenal cortical carcinoma is large, over 2 centimeters on the slide; about 50 percent are functional; it is highly malignant, infiltrative and can metastasize, with more severe symptoms than an adenoma. Most virilizing adrenal neoplasms are carcinomas. Pheochromocytoma The medulla is made of chromaffin cells, neuroendocrine cells, and a pheochromocytoma is a tumor of these neural crest chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla. It secretes catecholamines, so the patient has sweating, palpitations, paroxysmal attacks and hypertension; he added arrhythmia and a fast heart rate. Grossly, the bright golden cortex is pushed to the side by a pinkish-red medullary mass. Under the microscope the cells form nests, or balls, sitting next to each other. The German pathologist who first described them called the pattern Zellballen, which means cell balls. The classic "rule of 10s": 10 percent occur in familial syndromes: MEN, neurofibromatosis, von Hippel-Lindau and Sturge-Weber. 10 percent are extra-adrenal: the organ of Zuckerkandl or the carotid body, where they are called paragangliomas. 10 percent are bilateral. 10 percent are malignant. He warned that these numbers have stayed the same for over 20 years and may not be accurate: "could be true, could be not." Learn them as the slide gives them. Neuroblastoma In children, instead of a pheochromocytoma, the medulla can give rise to neuroblastoma, a very aggressive malignant childhood tumor. About 80 percent occur under age 5. It can arise anywhere in the sympathetic nervous system, most often in the abdomen, from the adrenal medulla or the retroperitoneal sympathetic ganglia, and it metastasizes to bone, liver, lung and lymph nodes. It is hard to survive, and he called it very rare, a tumor of the pediatric age group. Under the microscope it looks primitive: whenever you hear the word "blast," it means the precursor, the immature form of a cell. Between the small primitive cells is a pink fibrillary material that resembles glial brain tissue. Adults have their own form at the skull base: olfactory neuroblastoma, which grows in the olfactory cleft in the roof of the nose. It is also very aggressive and can show the same glial-like matrix and primitive cells. The pattern to carry into the exam Almost every question in this lecture is the same question: which hormone is high or low, and what is its driver doing? In primary disease the gland acts on its own and its driver is shut off by feedback: high calcium with high PTH that should have been suppressed, high cortisol with low ACTH, high aldosterone with low renin, low cortisol with high ACTH. In secondary disease the driver is the cause, and the two move together: renal failure pushing PTH up, ACTH from a pituitary or lung tumor pushing cortisol up, renal artery stenosis pushing renin and aldosterone up. And when the hormone is high but nothing happens, as in pseudohypoparathyroidism, the target organ is the problem.
